In the Septuagint it appears 371 times, almost always rendering Hebrew בָּנָה ("to build"), 292 times. Beyond the literal, the lexica note a figurative sense of building up character or encouraging—"edify"—which surfaces in renderings like "edified."

Everyday Koine papyri confirm the plain literal sense — one document from 126 BC uses it for building a dovecote, another for building a fountain.

prose.article: οἰκουμένη is literally "the land being inhabited," the populated world, and in the Byzantine NT it is rendered "world" 11 of 16 times (69%) and "earth" twice (13%). A papyrus announcing Nero's accession (P Oxy VII.1021, A.D. 54) calls him "the expectation and hope of the οἰκουμένη," showing how naturally the word stood for the Roman world. In the Septuagint it appears 45 times, most often translating the Hebrew tevel, "world."

prose.def: Describing a woman who watches over and stays at home, a keeper of the household.
prose.article: This adjective combines "house" (οἶκος) with the idea of guarding or keeping, describing someone who looks after the home. It appears only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Titus 2:5) and not at all in the SBL critical text, where editors prefer the closely related οἰκουργός ("house-worker"). In the Septuagint it appears 6 times, mostly translating the Hebrew word for a freewill offering (נְדָבָה, 4×), pointing toward something voluntarily declared or pledged.

prose.def: By common consent or admittedly — pointing to something everyone agrees is true beyond dispute.
prose.article: This adverb, built from the verb meaning "to confess" or "agree," signals that what follows is acknowledged by everyone as true. It appears just once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 3:16, where the King James Version renders it "without controversy." Everyday Koine papyri from the 2nd century B.C. use the word in legal contexts to mean "admittedly" — for example, where a person's own testimony makes a charge plainly undeniable. Abbott-Smith also notes an older sense, "as agreed" or "conformably with," though the New Testament use carries the "by common consent" meaning.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament and is absorbed into the surrounding phrasing rather than translated by a single English word, so its precise force rests largely on the papyri and lexical evidence.

prose.def: A connecting word meaning "yet," "nevertheless," or "even," signaling a contrast or exception to what was just said.
prose.article: This little connecting word adds a sense of "yet" or "nevertheless," marking something that holds true despite what came before. prose.def: A dream experienced while sleeping, especially one through which a divine message is given.
prose.article: Ὄναρ means a dream — the kind you have while asleep. In the New Testament it appears only 6 times, all in Matthew, and always in the phrase κατ᾽ ὄναρ, "in a dream" (as when angels warn Joseph or the Magi). The apparent multiple "senses" in the data are really just one meaning: the measured renderings ("dream," "after a dream," "Magi a dream") are all fragments of that same fixed phrase. One interesting wrinkle: in votive inscriptions the same phrase κατ᾽ ὄναρ tends to mean "in consequence of a dream" rather than "during a dream," and the ancient grammarian Photius even branded the construction as thoroughly "barbarous."
prose.caution: All 6 occurrences sit inside one fixed phrase in a single book, and the supposed separate senses are really phrase fragments rather than distinct meanings.

prose.def: A time-marker meaning "when" or "at the time that," linking one event to another.
prose.article: ὁπότε is a connecting word meaning "when" — it ties an action to the moment something else happened. In classical Greek it carried the sense of "whenever" (as in Homer), but in everyday Koine papyri it had softened to simply "when," and the New Testament follows this later usage in its single occurrence (Luke 6:3, where it introduces David's action when he was hungry). A nice papyrus parallel is P Oxy 243, dated A.D. 79, which uses ὁπότε περιῆν to mean "when she was alive."
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, so its biblical range cannot be measured beyond that single verse.
